history.heading: Antiquity and the medieval kingdom
paragraphs: The Adriatic coast of Croatia was home to Illyrian tribes and Greek colonies before becoming part of the Roman Empire. The Roman emperor Diocletian built his retirement palace in Split around 300 CE; the old town of Split grew within its walls.

Croats settled the region in the 7th century and adopted Christianity. The Kingdom of Croatia was established under Tomislav, crowned around 925. In 1102 Croatia entered a personal union with Hungary, keeping its own parliament (Sabor) and nobility.

history.heading: Habsburgs, Venice and Ottomans
paragraphs: Venice controlled much of the Dalmatian coast for centuries, while the Republic of Ragusa (Dubrovnik) remained an independent maritime republic until 1808. After the Ottoman victory at Mohács in 1526, Croatia came under the Habsburgs, and a Military Frontier was created against the Ottomans.
In the 19th century the Croatian National Revival promoted language and identity. After the First World War Croatia became part of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, later Yugoslavia.

history.heading: Second World War and Yugoslavia
paragraphs: During the Second World War the Axis created the Independent State of Croatia, ruled by the fascist Ustaše, which killed hundreds of thousands of Serbs, Jews and Roma, notably at the Jasenovac camp. Many Croats joined the communist partisans led by Josip Broz Tito, who was himself born in Croatia.
After the war Croatia was a republic within socialist Yugoslavia. The "Croatian Spring" movement for greater autonomy in 1971 was suppressed.

history.heading: Independence
paragraphs: Croatia declared independence on 25 June 1991. The Croatian War of Independence followed, as Serb rebels backed by the Yugoslav army took control of about a quarter of the country, besieging Vukovar and shelling Dubrovnik. In 1995 Croatian military operations retook most of the territory, and many Serbs fled.
Croatia joined NATO in 2009 and the European Union in 2013. It adopted the euro and joined the Schengen area on 1 January 2023.

culture.heading: Language and religion
paragraphs: Croatian is a South Slavic language written in the Latin alphabet; the medieval Glagolitic script is a cherished part of heritage. Most Croats are Catholic, and the Church has played an important role in national identity.
Dubrovnik, Split, Plitvice Lakes National Park and the Euphrasian Basilica in Poreč are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

culture.heading: Traditions and inventions
paragraphs: Klapa, a cappella singing from Dalmatia, is recognised by UNESCO. The necktie (cravat) derives its name from Croatian soldiers in 17th-century France. Inventor Nikola Tesla was born in Croatia, and the Dalmatian dog is named after the region.

Cuisine varies from Mediterranean dishes on the coast, such as seafood, olive oil and peka (food slow-cooked under a bell), to hearty continental food inland. Football is a passion; Croatia reached the World Cup final in 2018, with Luka Modrić as star player.

politics.heading: Parliamentary republic
paragraphs: Croatia is a parliamentary republic. The prime minister leads the government, which depends on the unicameral Sabor, while the directly elected president is head of state and commander-in-chief. The centre-right Croatian Democratic Union (HDZ) and the centre-left Social Democratic Party are the largest parties.
Croatia is a member of the EU, NATO, the eurozone and Schengen. Relations with Serbia and Bosnia and Herzegovina remain shaped by the wars of the 1990s.

economy.heading: Tourism and services
paragraphs: Tourism is a major pillar of the economy, contributing a large share of GDP, with millions of visitors to the Adriatic coast and its more than a thousand islands. Other sectors include shipbuilding, food processing, pharmaceuticals, IT and energy.

EU membership brought investment and funds. Challenges include population decline through emigration, labour shortages filled by foreign workers, and dependence on seasonal tourism. The currency is the euro.
